paper_title: AMLworld-Compact: Importance-Weighted Downsampling for Cost-Effective LLM Evaluation and Error Diagnosis

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Evaluating large language models (LLMs) on AMLworld's smallest test splits is costly because each of over a million targets requires a separate graph prompt. Sampling reduces this cost, but small balanced subsets change unweighted precision and F1. We introduce AMLworld-Compact, an evaluation set that retains every illicit test transaction and samples benign transactions from supervised-score strata. Its HT-Coreset protocol reduces evaluation targets by 271x and 611x on HI-Small and LI-Small. Horvitz-Thompson weights give unbiased full-test confusion-count estimates for fixed predictions; recall is exact, while precision and F1 are ratio estimates. In a held-out study using Graph Feature Preprocessor (GFP) features, one boosted-tree family defines strata for evaluating the other over 500 draws per configuration. At the released sizes, F1 RMSE is 0.00-2.58 percentage points versus 4.44-7.41 for uniform sampling with HT weights; conservative intervals remain broad. Under the evaluated graph prompts, seven open-weight LLMs have weighted precision near the predict-all-illicit baseline. In an outcome-stratified audit of 1,000 HI-Small few-shot outputs from one run per model, lexical checks pass for 84.5% of correct and 56.2% of incorrect binary verdicts, so these markers do not establish correctness. We release the evaluation sets, construction code, and audit tools at https://huggingface.co/datasets/typhoon-ai/AMLworldCompactEval and https://github.com/nat-nischw/AMLworld-Compact.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Anti-money laundering (AML) detection asks whether transaction belongs to illicit activity. The evidence can span several accounts and transfers: gather-scatter pattern, for example, collects funds at one account before redistributing them. large language model (LLM) can receive this neighborhood as graph text, but evaluating each transaction 1 typhoon-ai/AMLworldCompactEval github.com/nat-nischw/AMLworld-Compact separately requires one prompt per target. The test partitions of AMLworlds two smallest splits (Altman et al., 2023) each contain over million transactions, with illicit rates of 0.12% on HI-Small and 0.05% on LI-Small. single pass on either split requires over million graph prompts; comparing models and prompt variants multiplies this workload. small class-proportional sample contains few illicit cases, limiting recall and typology analysis. balanced sample increases their share but changes unweighted precision and F1. Prior exploratory work (Pirmorad, 2025) evaluates LLMs on small balanced AMLworld subset; those scores reflect its enriched illicit proportion. The challenge is to reduce model calls while keeping rare cases available for diagnosis and estimating detection at full-test prevalence. We introduce AMLworld-Compact, constructed with HT-Coreset. The protocol retains every illicit test edge, uses supervised scores to identify difficult benign cases, and samples the remaining benign edges within difficulty strata. Known inclusion probabilities give HorvitzThompson (HT) weights (Horvitz and Thompson, 1952) for estimating full-test confusion counts. The weights account for unsampled benign cases; unweighted counts describe errors on the selected cases. These two summaries use the same selected targets and predictions (Figure 1); precision and F1 are ratio estimates, with possible finite-sample bias. The released sets contain 3,753 HI-Small and 2,268 LI-Small targets, reducing target counts by 271 and 611. Each target has GFP features (Blanuša et al., 2024) and typed-subgraph prompt extracted from the full graph: selecting fewer targets does not reduce the neighborhood available to each selected case. Our contributions are: An evaluation set with full-test reference. The released targets, inclusion weights, features, and graph strings let subsequent models use the same cases and estimate metrics for the same population. We compare 12 budgets and 7 alternative samplers, then test sampling error and interval coverage with the evaluated booster family held out of construction, over 500 draws per configuration (Section 3). LLM evaluation and error analysis. Seven open-weight LLMs with the original prompts have weighted precision near full-test illicit prevalence. We analyze MLLLM error overlap and find that lexical checks pass for over half of the incorrect binary verdicts in the audit sample. supplementary control shows that the labelderived route accounts for most of the apparent hybrid gain (Sections 4 and 5).

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: LLM evaluation on AML graphs. Pirmorad (2025) explores in-context learning on small balanced AMLworld subset. We reuse their typedgraph prompt template with our own neighborhoods and demonstrations. Our evaluation set adds different population reference: inclusion weights estimate full-test detection counts despite the subsets enriched illicit proportion. We study sampling error and use the selected cases to analyze detection and written outputs. Graph inputs and graph retrieval. Chen et al. (2024) study LLMs as feature enhancers and direct predictors for node classification; Fatemi et al. (2024) examine how text encodings affect graph reasoning. Our task is transaction classification from fixed k-hop graph presented as text. GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) instead retrieves information over graph index. Retrieval quality and reasoning over supplied neighborhood are distinct evaluation problems. Efficient evaluation and coreset selection. tinyBenchmarks (Maia Polo et al., 2024) and metabench (Kipnis et al., 2025) include latentability methods that use prior model responses to estimate full-benchmark scores from small test subsets. Here, known transaction labels identify rare class that we retain in full; supervised scores allocate the benign sampling budget. CRAIG (Mirzasoleiman et al., 2020) and CCS (Zheng et al., 2023) select training coresets, whereas our subset is used for evaluation. Fogliato et al. (2024) study stratified sampling with design-based and model-assisted estimators for classification evaluation. Our Neymanallocation baseline (Neyman, 1934) adapts their framework to binary classification, sampling both classes; HT-Coreset retains all illicit edges and weights sampled benign edges. The comparisons in the next section test these choices at matched budgets.

sections.title: 3 Constructing AMLworld-Compact
sections.content: HT-Coreset takes the full test partition and supervised scores as inputs. It selects transaction targets and records their inclusion probabilities for subsequent evaluation.

sections.title: 3.1 Setting
sections.content: Evaluation population. We use HI-Small and LI-Small, the two smallest splits of AMLworld (Altman et al., 2023). Its labeled synthetic transaction graphs let us compare sampled estimates with known full-test metrics. Each edge is labeled illicit or benign; illicit edges may carry one of 8 typology annotations (Appendix A). We first partition the source CSV rows 60/20/20 for training, validation, and testing in file order. HTCoreset then selects targets only from the test partition. Timestamps overlap across partitions, so this split is not strictly chronological. The released sets use one illicit edge to two benign edges (1:2), the smallest budget meeting our tested construction criterion. Construction scores. Scores guide the benign budget toward likely false positives, which can low illicit prevastrongly affect precision at lence. We use LightGBM (Ke et al., 2017), XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin, 2016), and GCPAL (Lu and Wang, 2024) with Graph Feature Preprocessor (GFP) features (Blanuša et al., 2024) to define the strata. The boosters train on the training partition. The archived GCPAL checkpoints use random fine-tuning split that overlaps the test set. We retain the frozen construction design and its inclusion weights; task comparisons use only the two boosters. Appendix D.6 gives feature dimensions, architectures, training settings, and split provenance.

sections.title: 3.2 Class-Proportional Downsampling
sections.content: Naïve Coreset preserves the class ratio while stratifying illicit edges by typology and difficulty. At small budgets, few illicit edges remain for recall estimation. The smallest feasible draw found for HI-Small in our constrained search contains 641K edges (absolute F1 deviation at most 5 pp; Appendix D.3). Retaining all illicit cases instead allows much smaller benign budget, with importance weights accounting for unequal benign-edge selection probabilities.

sections.title: 3.3 HT-Coreset
sections.content: Stage 1: retain all illicit cases. Keeping every illicit edge preserves recall information and all 8 typologies rather than relying on small minority sample. Stage 2: allocate the benign budget. To retain likely false positives, we score each edge with p(e), the mean across 3 scorers and 5 seeds. We define the difficulty score as d(e) = 1 2 p(e) 0.5. Difficulty is highest at mean probability of 0.5. Hard negatives are benign edges with mean probabilities of at least 0.40 on HI-Small or 0.24 on LI-Small. These cutoffs are half the ensembles respective operating thresholds. Up to 30% of the benign budget is reserved for this high-score stratum. We use the remaining budget to sample other benign edges from three difficulty strata (terciles). These four benign strata give every benign edge positive inclusion probability. At the released budgets, all hard negatives fit, with 363 on HI-Small (14.5% of its benign sample) and 269 on LI-Small (17.8%). We select the smallest of 12 benign budgets whose mean absolute HT-weighted deviations in precision (P ), recall (R), and F1 are each at most 5 percentage points (pp) over 50 draws. The selected budget is twice the illicit count, giving the 1:2 ratio used for LLM evaluation. This is the maximum reduction among the budgets tested. Stage 3: estimate full-test counts. Each selected edge receives weight we = 1/πe, the inverse of its inclusion probability. Retained illicit edges have weight one. Summing weights over TP, FP, and FN gives estimated full-test confusion counts. Precision, recall, and F1 are computed from these counts. For fixed predictions and known positive inclusion probabilities, the counts are unbiased. Complete illicit retention makes recall exact; precision and F1 are ratio estimates with possible finite-sample bias and sampling variance (Appendix D.2). Algorithm 1 gives the procedure. Two summaries of the same predictions. Both reports use the same targets selected by HT-Coreset and the same predictions. HT-weighted scoring estimates full-test performance; unweighted scoring sets we = 1 to describe the enriched subset. predictor that flags every edge has 33.3% precision and 50.0% F1 on the released 1:2 subset, but 0.123% precision and 0.246% F1 on the full HISmall test split. HT weighting recovers the full-test predict-all reference.

sections.title: 4 LLM Evaluation
sections.content: The retained targets make repeated model and prompt comparisons possible with thousands of requests per pass. We ask whether the LLMs distinguish illicit from benign transactions and identify illicit typologies. Detection is assessed against predict-all-illicit reference, which achieves high recall without distinguishing cases.

sections.title: 5 Diagnosing LLM Outputs
sections.content: The detection results motivate two questions: do LLMs recover cases missed by ML, and do observable trace markers help distinguish correct answers? Error decompositions and trace analyses use the available records from the run labeled 42; the label-concentration figure pools all five runs. Unless marked HT, counts and rates describe the selected cases or the stated audit sample. Written traces need not faithfully represent internal computation (Turpin et al., 2023; Tutek et al., 2025).

sections.title: 5.1 Decomposing ML and LLM Errors
sections.content: The HI-Small ML reference has 84.8% precision and 56.8% recall. Most zero-shot LLMs have much higher recall but flag nearly three times the true illicit count (Appendix F.3). To examine complementarity, Table 4 groups edges by whether ML, GPT-OSS-120B, both, or neither gives the correct binary verdict. Ground-truth labels determine these groups. Of 2,123 ML-only-correct edges, 2,064 are benign; the groups mean ML score is 0.08. Of 433 LLM-only-correct edges, 410 are illicit; the groups mean ML score is 0.13. Both means are far below the 0.80 ML threshold. The LLM recovers missed illicit cases but also flags benign cases with low ML scores. useful router would have to distinguish these groups using observable information; their ground-truth-defined means do not give such rule. Full transitions and per-typology results are in Appendices F.1 and F.2.

sections.title: 5.3 Lexical Checks and Answer Correctness
sections.content: We test whether traces that name structural features, candidate typologies, and supporting markers are more likely to accompany correct verdict. The audit contains 1,000 outcome-stratified HI-Small few-shot records across seven models, including 148 empty traces. The original rubric, motivated by step-level process supervision (Lightman et al., 2024), checks Parse (features), Recall (typologies), Match (structural markers), and Conclude (reference verdict and, when illicit, typology). Regex rules and three API judges score this sample (Appendix H.1). For the correctness comparison, revised regex checks require at least two feature categories, two typology-name strings, and two marker categories for every verdict. This removes the original Match rules automatic pass for nonempty benign verdicts. We repeat the checks on the first 8,000 characters to match the judges text window, using the same frozen model outputs. Thus, the markers are more common in correct outputs but also occur in many incorrect ones; passing them is insufficient for correctness. Three human raters assess separate 28-record sample, one record per model in each of four outcome groups. Match agreement is low (κ = 0.10); Conclude uses shared parser rule. The API judges also receive no transaction graph. These checks assess rubric application within the samples and cannot independently validate graph grounding or estimate population failure rates (Appendices H.2 and H.3).

sections.title: 5.4 A Supplementary Routing Diagnostic
sections.content: The error overlap motivates testing how much hybrid comparisons gain comes from the LLM versus the selected route. Doubt Triage (DT) consults an LLM on ML-negative edges in the weight-one stratum (all illicit edges and retained hard-negative benign edges) and uses ML elsewhere. Its best zero-shot detection F1, averaged over five runs, is 87.3% on HI-Small (ML: 68.1%) and 84.9% on LI-Small (ML: 28.6%). An always-illicit answer on the same route, without LLM calls, also reaches 87.3% and 84.9%. The route therefore accounts for most of the apparent gain. Because it uses label-derived strata, DT does not establish rule for selecting cases at deployment. Appendix G.1 reports the control and tested score-only routes.

sections.title: 6 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.content: AMLworld-Compact enables model and prompt comparisons with thousands of evaluation targets while retaining every illicit test case. To reuse it, align predictions to the released case IDs and apply the supplied inclusion weights to confusion counts before computing precision and F1. Report HTweighted estimates for full-test performance and unweighted errors for the selected cases, stating which input version was evaluated. new labeled transaction graph requires its own strata and inclusion probabilities. The construction checks show metric agreement for the ensemble used to select targets. Holding out GFP booster family gives lower point error than uniform benign sampling at matched budgets, although conservative intervals remain broad. This supports the benign allocation for the tested families while leaving transfer to other predictors open. With the original graph prompts, the evaluated LLMs flag many benign transactions; high recall accompanies precision near full-test illicit prevalence. Demonstration gains are more consistent for typology identification than for detection. Prompt comparisons should report these tasks separately. In the audit sample, lexical checks pass more often for correct answers and also for over half of incorrect binary verdicts. Trace audits should compare check outcomes with answer correctness rather than treat pass as evidence that the answer is supported by the graph. paired comparison of original and target-marked inputs, holding models, demonstrations, and scoring fixed, could measure sensitivity to the combined input changes. The supplementary frontier probe uses different protocol and does not provide that comparison (Appendix I.3).

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: The main LLM evaluation covers seven openweight models on two small synthetic AMLworld splits with one graph-to-text pipeline. Generalizability to larger graphs and real banking data remains untested. The evaluated inputs do not consistently identify and include the target transaction (Section 3.4), so their errors cannot be attributed solely to model reasoning. The CSV-order partitions have overlapping timestamps and do not establish strictly prospective ML performance. The task ML reference and DT use thresholds selected on full-test labels, making comparisons at these thresholds exploratory. LLMs were evaluated at one coreset size and one 50-neighbor serialization cap. Sampling uncertainty conditions on the frozen design and predictions; it has not been checked against full-test LLM predictions or independently evaluated coreset draws (Appendix D.2). The held-out-family study tests two related GFP boosters and does not establish transfer to unrelated predictors. Trace-level findings use the available run, and their stability across runs is untested. The 28record human check assesses rubric application on an outcome-stratified sample (Appendix H.3).

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: AMLworld (Altman et al., 2023) is synthetic: its account identifiers, amounts, and relationships do not expose real customers. The supplementary Elliptic experiment uses public Bitcoin transactions (Appendix D.8). The intended use is better evaluation of AML detection, but examples of laundering patterns could also help attempts to evade detection. False positives can burden legitimate customers and compliance teams; the reported over-prediction does not support LLM-only deployment. DT uses label-informed evaluation strata, and retaining ML in the loop does not establish deployment safety. Release licenses and the code-only Elliptic distribution are documented in Appendix A. AI Usage Statement. The authors used AI assistants (Claude and GPT-class models) for manuscript editing and code review. The authors are responsible for the experimental design, interpretation, and final manuscript.
